articles.title: One CLAUDE.md Doesn't Fit Every Project: Split Your Templates by Situation, Not by Stack
articles.excerpt: Most CLAUDE.md templates you'll find are organized by stack: one for React, one for Laravel, one for Rails. When I started using Claude Code for freelance client work, I collected a few of those — and…
articles.body: Most CLAUDE.md templates you'll find are organized by stack: one for React, one for Laravel, one for Rails. When I started using Claude Code for freelance client work, I collected a few of those — and then barely used them. The problem wasn't the stack sections. It was that the working rules I actually needed had almost nothing to do with the framework. They depended on the situation the project was in: Am I building something new , where the conventions are mine to set? Am I maintaining code I didn't write , where the priority is not breaking a live system? Is this billable client work , where scope, approvals, and handover matter as much as the code? Same stack, three completely different rule sets. So I reorganized my templates around situations instead.

articles.body: A field journal from a non-developer who shipped a functionnal multi-user app alone, with AI, in three weeks. Read this first I am not a software engineer. I build tender responses for a living — spreadsheets, technical memos, cost models. In autumn 2026 I decided to turn a personal life-management app I had been using alone into something other people could sign up for. I had the thing working on my laptop already. I thought the remaining work was "put it on the internet." That is the sentence this guide exists to disarm. What follows is not a tutorial. There are thousands of tutorials and they all stop at the same place: the happy path, on your machine, with one user, with your own data, with no money involved.

articles.title: One pipeline, one document, and 46 minutes of stalled deploys
articles.excerpt: Friday 13 November 2026, just before six in the evening, UTC. Pipelines on Harness prod3 started hanging. Not all of them, and not all at once. Some slowed to a crawl. Some would not start at all. Som…
articles.body: Friday 13 November 2026, just before six in the evening, UTC. Pipelines on Harness prod3 started hanging. Not all of them, and not all at once. Some slowed to a crawl. Some would not start at all. Some sat there long enough that the platform gave up on them, aborting any execution that had been stuck for more than five minutes. Two customers reported the slowdown. The rest of the platform looked fine. There had been no deploy to blame. No config change, no bad release, no spike in traffic that anyone could point at. The pipelines were just... stopping. That is the kind of failure that makes an on-call engineer reach for a second coffee, because the usual suspects are all innocent and the clock is running. This is the story of what they found, and it is a story about a single document.

articles.title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Which Fixes Your LLM Problem?
articles.excerpt: Originally published on DevToolHub. RAG vs fine-tuning comes down to one question: what is wrong with the model's answers? If it lacks facts, such as your docs or last week's changes, use RAG. If it k…
articles.body: Originally published on DevToolHub . RAG vs fine-tuning comes down to one question: what is wrong with the model's answers? If it lacks facts, such as your docs or last week's changes, use RAG. If it knows enough but answers in the wrong format or tone, fine-tune. I tested the first case locally: a 3B model got 0 of 10 questions right about an invented runbook, then 10 of 10 once the right passages were in the prompt. One 2026 detail changes the usual advice. OpenAI's own docs say its fine-tuning platform is winding down. It is closed to new users, and existing users can create training jobs only until January 6, 2027. On hosted models, retrieval is now the default path.

articles.title: Did your last release make reviews worse? Compare ratings and complaints by app version
articles.excerpt: A release goes out, and a week later someone asks whether it made things better or worse. The store's average rating will not tell you: it covers years of reviews and barely moves. You want the review…
articles.body: A release goes out, and a week later someone asks whether it made things better or worse. The store's average rating will not tell you: it covers years of reviews and barely moves. You want the reviews written for the new version next to those for the previous one, with a competitor alongside. This post builds that table: rating distribution, complaint themes and developer reply rate, per version and store. Everything is aggregate; no reviewer names are needed. Why this is harder than it looks The store average is the wrong number. It is lifetime; reviews for one version are a small, recent slice. Only one store reliably gives the version. Every Apple review in the public feed carries one.

articles.title: Cheapest Object Storage Service: Storing User Documents with Recovery Boundaries
articles.excerpt: Object Storage Boundaries: A Guide to Restoring Tenant Logistics Records The cheapest object store is not the one with the smallest storage line item. It is the one whose recovery boundary you can exp…
articles.body: Object Storage Boundaries: A Guide to Restoring Tenant Logistics Records The cheapest object store is not the one with the smallest storage line item. It is the one whose recovery boundary you can explain after a retry, a duplicate message, and a partially completed restore. For a logistics system holding documents per tenant, I would choose private object storage, keep snapshot truth in an application database, and make restore workers idempotent. The vendor choice comes after that.

articles.title: Building a Multi-Turn AI Chatbot with Python and Google Gemini
articles.excerpt: Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how developers build intelligent applications. Instead of training models from scratch, developers can integrate existing AI models into their applications us…
articles.body: Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how developers build intelligent applications. Instead of training models from scratch, developers can integrate existing AI models into their applications using APIs. Recently, I worked on a hands-on project to understand this process by developing a multi-turn AI chatbot using Python and Google's Gemini API. The project helped me explore an important aspect of AI application development: how to maintain meaningful conversations between users and AI models. Why Build a Multi-Turn Chatbot? A basic chatbot sends a user message to an AI model and displays the generated response. However, this approach does not automatically maintain conversation continuity. Consider a simple interaction: User: My name is Lakshmi. AI: Nice to meet you!

articles.title: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?
articles.excerpt: Conspiracy theories surround the odd-looking appearance of a shadow seen in the final images captured by Phobos 2, the Soviet Union’s last mission into deep space.
articles.body: On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft.

articles.excerpt: Three stars, 28 light-years, and one big cosmic mystery.
articles.body: A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system. "We were actually looking for planets ," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement . "Instead, we found something much more surprising." So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years . Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour.
